framework.name: PDCA / Deming Cycle
framework.one_liner: Turns a change into an experiment: a prediction written before the work, a trial small enough to be wrong in, a comparison against the prediction, and a decision to standardise or turn the cycle again.

slots.label: Phase
slots.description: Plan, Do, Check and Act: the four positions of the cycle itself. Scaffolding that exists before any source is read, so these nodes carry provenance schema, no quote and no confidence.

slots.label: Hypothesis
slots.description: Plan: what is expected to happen and why. Written down in a disciplined cycle; almost never stated in the wild, which is why this is the slot an LLM most often has to derive.

slots.label: Pilot
slots.description: Do: the contained trial actually run - which change, on which population, for how long. Normally stated, because people narrate what they did.

slots.label: Metric
slots.description: Check: what the trial was read against. A fact when it was agreed before the trial; derived when numbers are reported and no measure was ever declared.

slots.label: Measurement
slots.description: Check: the observed value or outcome, including a refusal or a verdict from the pilot's users. Usually stated, often the only part of the cycle that is.

slots.label: Decision
slots.description: Act: standardise, adjust and run again, or abandon. The stated decision is a fact; the rule it standardises and the decision the measurement implies but nobody took are derived, and that is where the opportunity sits.

relations.label: in phase
relations.description: this node belongs to that phase of the cycle; scaffolding, not a claim about the world

relations.label: advances to
relations.description: the cycle turns from this phase to the next; the loop's own arrow, part of the framework rather than the source

relations.label: tests
relations.description: the pilot tests this hypothesis; the edge that makes a trial an experiment rather than a build

relations.label: measured by
relations.description: the pilot is read against this metric

relations.label: yields
relations.description: this produced that value: a metric yields its measurement, and where no metric was ever declared the pilot yields the number directly

relations.label: leads to
relations.description: this result drove the next step: a measurement to the decision it produced, or a baseline to the hypothesis it prompted

relations.label: restarts
relations.description: the decision turns the cycle again with a new hypothesis

examples.title: Packing line seal failures: one pilot on one shift
examples.summary: A packing department's improvement note: a written prediction about the sealing jaws, a trial confined to one line, one shift and five days, two measures agreed before the trial, and a standardisation that goes exactly as far as the pilot and no further.

insights.short: Given a packing department's note where twelve per cent of Line 2's cartons failed the seal test, the engineer predicted fifteen more degrees would cut failures under three per cent, a five-day night-shift trial reached 2.1 per cent while scorching rose one to four per ten thousand, and the team standardised on Line 2 and scheduled Line 5, applying PDCA / Deming Cycle we derived that standardising traded a fourfold rise in scorching for a sixfold cut in failures, that the mechanism named a fast line while the trial ran the slow shift, and that Line 5 carries an unwritten prediction; the reader gains the trade the memo never weighs and the speed assumption a clean cycle hides.
insights.long:
The facts. A packing department's week 14 improvement note records that twelve per cent of the biscuit cartons off Line 2 fail the seal test and have been re-sealed by hand for a year. The engineer reads the data as the sealing jaws running too cool when the line is fast, and expects that raising the jaw temperature by fifteen degrees will cut seal failures to under three per cent without scorching the film. Rather than change all six lines, the team ran the higher temperature on Line 2 only, on the night shift, which runs the line slower, for five days, with two measures agreed in advance: seal failures fell from twelve to 2.1 per cent and scorching rejects rose from one to four per ten thousand. The team wrote the temperature into Line 2's standard work instruction and scheduled the same trial on Line 5, where the film is thinner.

The method. PDCA separates the prediction, the contained trial, the measures agreed before the result, and a decision that reaches exactly as far as the trial did. This memo fills every slot; what it leaves thin is the Act phase, which records two numbers and weighs neither, and the next Plan, which is scheduled but never written.

What we derived. Standardising accepted a fourfold rise in scorching rejects, one to four per ten thousand, as the price of cutting seal failures roughly sixfold, a judgement the decision encodes and the memo never states (86%). The next turn of the cycle tests whether the same fifteen degrees holds where the film is thinner and scorches more easily, a prediction implied by scheduling the Line 5 trial but not written down (74%). And the stated mechanism names a fast line while the trial ran only the slower night shift, so that the setting works at day-shift speed is assumed by the standardisation rather than tested by it (68%). The reader gains, in place of a business idea, the unweighed trade and the untested condition that a tidy improvement note carries past its own standard.

source.title: Improvement note, packing department, week 14
source.attribution: Synthetic scenario in the genre Deming taught from 1950 and Shewhart's 1939 cycle before it: a predicted effect, a small-scale trial, a comparison against the prediction, and a standard rewritten only for what was tested.
source.text:
Improvement note, packing department, week 14.

Twelve per cent of the biscuit cartons coming off Line 2 fail the seal test, and the department has been re-sealing them by hand for a year.

The engineer's reading of the data is that the sealing jaws run too cool when the line is fast, so she expects that raising the jaw temperature by fifteen degrees will cut seal failures to under three per cent without scorching the film.

Rather than change all six lines, the team ran the higher temperature on Line 2 only, on the night shift, for five production days, and logged every carton.

The night shift runs Line 2 slower than the day shift does.

The two measures agreed before the trial were the seal failure rate per thousand cartons and the number of cartons rejected for scorched film.

Over the five days the seal failure rate fell from twelve per cent to two point one per cent, and four cartons in ten thousand were rejected for scorching, against a baseline of one in ten thousand.

The team wrote the new temperature into the standard work instruction for Line 2 and scheduled the same five-day trial on Line 5, where the film is thinner and scorches more easily.

annotations.text: prediction written before the trial, measures agreed before the trial

nodes.label: Plan
nodes.text: Plan: state what is expected to happen and why, and decide in advance what would count as evidence.

nodes.label: Do
nodes.text: Do: run the change on a small scale, contained so that a bad result costs little and a good result can be traced to the change.

nodes.label: Check (Study)
nodes.text: Check, which Deming later renamed Study: compare what happened with what was predicted, using the measures agreed beforehand.

nodes.label: Act
nodes.text: Act: standardise the change, adjust it and run the cycle again, or abandon it - and then turn the cycle.

nodes.label: 12% of cartons fail the seal test
nodes.text: Twelve per cent of the cartons coming off Line 2 fail the seal test, and the department has been re-sealing the failures by hand for a year. This is the baseline the Plan phase starts from.
nodes.source_quote: Twelve per cent of the biscuit cartons coming off Line 2 fail the seal test, and the department has been re-sealing them by hand for a year.

nodes.label: +15 degrees cuts failures under 3%
nodes.text: The engineer expects that raising the jaw temperature by fifteen degrees will cut seal failures to under three per cent without scorching the film, because the jaws run too cool when the line is fast.
nodes.source_quote: so she expects that raising the jaw temperature by fifteen degrees will cut seal failures to under three per cent without scorching the film

nodes.label: Assumed: it holds on the day shift
nodes.text: The trial ran on the night shift, which runs Line 2 slower than the day shift does. That the same setting works at day-shift speed is assumed by the standardisation, not tested by it.
nodes.rationale: The stated mechanism is that the jaws run too cool when the line is fast; the trial ran only on the slower shift, so the faster condition the mechanism names was never the one measured. The inference is a gap in the cycle, not a claim about the result.

nodes.label: Line 5 hypothesis: thinner film
nodes.text: The next turn of the cycle tests whether the same fifteen degrees holds where the film is thinner, which the memo says scorches more easily. That prediction is not written down; scheduling the trial implies it.
nodes.rationale: A trial is scheduled on Line 5 and the memo gives the reason the line differs (thinner film, scorches more easily). The hypothesis under test follows from the pairing, but nobody states it as an expectation.

nodes.label: Line 2, night shift, five days
nodes.text: Rather than change all six lines, the team ran the higher temperature on Line 2 only, on the night shift, for five production days, logging every carton.
nodes.source_quote: Rather than change all six lines, the team ran the higher temperature on Line 2 only, on the night shift, for five production days, and logged every carton.

nodes.label: Night shift runs Line 2 slower
nodes.text: The night shift runs Line 2 slower than the day shift does, so the pilot is contained in speed as well as in line, shift and duration.
nodes.source_quote: The night shift runs Line 2 slower than the day shift does.

nodes.label: Seal failure rate per 1,000
nodes.text: The seal failure rate per thousand cartons, one of the two measures agreed before the trial began.
nodes.source_quote: The two measures agreed before the trial were the seal failure rate per thousand cartons

nodes.label: Cartons rejected for scorching
nodes.text: The number of cartons rejected for scorched film: the measure that watches for the harm the change could do, agreed before the trial alongside the measure of the benefit.
nodes.source_quote: the number of cartons rejected for scorched film

nodes.label: 12% fell to 2.1%
nodes.text: Over the five days the seal failure rate fell from twelve per cent to two point one per cent, beating the prediction of under three per cent.
nodes.source_quote: Over the five days the seal failure rate fell from twelve per cent to two point one per cent

nodes.label: Scorching 1 to 4 per 10,000
nodes.text: Four cartons in ten thousand were rejected for scorching, against a baseline of one in ten thousand: the harm the second measure was watching for did occur.
nodes.source_quote: four cartons in ten thousand were rejected for scorching, against a baseline of one in ten thousand

nodes.label: Standardise on Line 2
nodes.text: The team wrote the new temperature into the standard work instruction for Line 2: the change is standardised exactly as far as the pilot reached, and no further.
nodes.source_quote: The team wrote the new temperature into the standard work instruction for Line 2

nodes.label: Run the same trial on Line 5
nodes.text: The team scheduled the same five-day trial on Line 5, where the film is thinner and scorches more easily, rather than rolling the setting out to the remaining lines.
nodes.source_quote: scheduled the same five-day trial on Line 5, where the film is thinner and scorches more easily

nodes.label: Accepted trade: 4x scorch, 6x seal
nodes.text: Standardising accepted a fourfold rise in scorching rejects, one to four per ten thousand, as the price of cutting seal failures roughly sixfold. The memo records both numbers and neither weighs them.
nodes.rationale: Arithmetic on the two measured values plus the fact that the team standardised anyway: 12 per cent to 2.1 per cent is close to a sixfold cut, one to four per ten thousand is a fourfold rise, and accepting the second to get the first is the judgement the decision encodes.

edges.source_quote: The engineer's reading of the data is that the sealing jaws run too cool when the line is fast
edges.label: reads the data

edges.rationale: The pilot changes exactly the variable the prediction names, by the amount it names; that the trial is the test of that prediction is forced by the pairing even though no sentence says so.

edges.source_quote: The two measures agreed before the trial were the seal failure rate per thousand cartons
edges.label: agreed before

edges.source_quote: The two measures agreed before the trial were the seal failure rate per thousand cartons and the number of cartons rejected for scorched film
edges.label: agreed before

edges.source_quote: the seal failure rate fell from twelve per cent to two point one per cent
four cartons in ten thousand were rejected for scorching, against a baseline of one in ten thousand

edges.rationale: The measured 2.1 per cent beats the predicted three per cent, and the standardisation follows in the next sentence; the memo never writes the because, so the link is a standard reading of adjacency plus the prediction being met.
The scorching result is the only reason a trade-off has to be weighed at all; the decision to standardise in spite of it is what makes the judgement visible.
The benefit side of the accepted trade is the sixfold cut in seal failures, so the trade-off judgement hangs on this measurement as much as on the scorching one.
Scheduling a second trial rather than rolling out is the cycle turning again; the hypothesis the new turn will test has to be reconstructed from the reason the memo gives for picking Line 5.

examples.title: Ramp Labs: two turns of one cycle on Ramp Sheets
examples.summary: Two Ramp Labs engineers narrate the loop that produced Ramp Sheets: workflow automations piloted on Ramp's own finance team and refused, a re-measurement that found 99 per cent of the work in a spreadsheet, a pivot, and then a public release reported in impressions with nothing to compare them against.

insights.short: Given Alex Shevchenko and Alex Stauffer's account on TBPN of how Ramp Labs built Ramp Sheets, where automations mined from the finance team's videos were refused as too black box, a sample of their Loom recordings showed a spreadsheet 99 per cent of the time, and the public release drew two million impressions and demand from founders with no finance team, applying PDCA / Deming Cycle we derived the predictions neither turn stated, the undeclared measures each pilot was read against, and a second Check no number could have failed; the opportunity that falls out is finance AI sold as a spreadsheet that writes the model, and an instant model layer for people who will never hire an analyst.
insights.long:
The facts. On TBPN on 24 November 2025, Alex Shevchenko of Ramp Labs said Ramp Sheets started as an experiment: the finance team's workflows were mined from video and rebuilt as Zapier and Retool automations, which it refused as too black box. Random points in its Loom recordings showed a spreadsheet 99 per cent of the time, so the team decided to meet finance where it works. Alex Stauffer said the public release a week earlier, made only to see how people would play with it, drew two million impressions and thousands of users; Shevchenko called founders, VCs and small-business owners without a finance team real demand.

The method. PDCA asks what was predicted, what was tried, what the result was read against, and what was decided. The source states both turns' pilots, numbers and pivot but neither prediction nor measure; the second Check reports reach with nothing to beat.

What we derived. The first pilot's unstated prediction was that the finance team would adopt the automations and stop working by hand (72%); the second turn's, that a spreadsheet needing no Google or Excel account would be used by non-customers (66%). The first pilot's implicit measure was adoption, with no target, so refusal is the whole result (70%); the release's was reach, with no threshold, so no number could have come out wrong (62%). The pivot standardises a rule the source stops short of: ship into the surface the work already happens on (62%). Opportunity: Finance and back-office AI sells better as a spreadsheet that writes the model than as an agent that replaces the spreadsheet: the wedge is the surface the work is already recorded on, which is checkable by sampling recordings of the work. The measurements also point at the population the release found rather than the finance team (58%). Opportunity: An underserved segment: founders, VCs and small-business owners with no finance team who need a pro-forma or budget model in minutes and today pay a consultant thousands for a one-off template - a templated, instantly generated model layer priced for people who will never hire an analyst.

source.episode_title: Reviewing the best AI apps, Anthropic unveils Claude 4.5 Opus (Doug DeMuro, Sholto Douglas, Quinn Slack, Alex Stauffer, Alex Shevchenko)

examples.why_this_episode: Alex Shevchenko and Alex Stauffer narrate a complete improvement cycle twice over: a contained pilot on one named population, a refusal, a deliberate re-measurement with a hard number, a stated pivot, and then a second turn whose Check phase is nothing but reported reach. Both of PDCA's provenance lessons are in one segment - the decision is quoted, the hypothesis never is.

annotations.text: turn 2 · public release, plus what turn 1 standardised
Check holds numbers but no declared target: the two metrics behind them are inferences

nodes.label: Plan
nodes.text: Plan: state what is expected to happen and why, and decide in advance what would count as evidence.

nodes.label: Do
nodes.text: Do: run the change on a small scale, contained so that a bad result costs little and a good result can be traced to the change.

nodes.label: Check (Study)
nodes.text: Check, which Deming later renamed Study: compare what happened with what was predicted, using the measures agreed beforehand.

nodes.label: Act
nodes.text: Act: standardise the change, adjust it and run the cycle again, or abandon it - and then turn the cycle.

nodes.label: Started out as an experiment
nodes.text: Ramp Sheets began as an experiment inside Ramp Labs, which runs everything as an experiment. The source states that an experiment was run; it never states what the experiment predicted.
nodes.source_quote: Well, originally this started out as an experiment, as everything within Ramp Labs is.

nodes.label: Contained to Ramp's finance team
nodes.text: The variations were tried on one population: Ramp's own internal finance team. The Do phase is contained to users the team sits next to.
nodes.source_quote: We've been trying out different variations of this, actually, just to try to help our own internal finance team.

nodes.label: Process mining from video
nodes.text: The first thing built was process mining: documenting the finance team's workflows from video so the team could hand them to software engineers.
nodes.source_quote: This initially was like process mining to document some of their workflows from video so that they can communicate better between each other into software engineers.

nodes.label: Zapier and Retool automations
nodes.text: From the mined processes the team built Zapier and Retool workflows to automate the finance team's work, and pushed the finance team to use them.
nodes.source_quote: And then we tried to take that piece and create like Zapier and, like retool workflows based on them to try to automate and we tried to get them to use it

nodes.label: Many iterations
nodes.text: The product reached its current form through many iterations: the cycle turned repeatedly before the spreadsheet existed.
nodes.source_quote: This has gone, as I said, through many iterations.

nodes.label: Released publicly last week
nodes.text: The spreadsheet was released publicly the week before the interview, open to anyone rather than to a contained set of users, and the response was immediate.
nodes.source_quote: So we released it last week and then the response was overwhelming.

nodes.label: Sampled their Loom recordings
nodes.text: After the rejection the team went back to the Loom recordings the finance team had given them and sampled random points in them. This is the one measure in the source that was deliberately taken.
nodes.source_quote: we like took a step back and tried to look through the looms of like all the information that they were giving to us

nodes.label: Too black box, no visibility
nodes.text: The finance team refused the automations: too black box, unusable, no visibility into what they did.
nodes.source_quote: and they were like no this is too black box we can't really use this we need visibility into it

nodes.label: 99% of Looms were a spreadsheet
nodes.text: Sampling random points in the recordings, 99 per cent of the time the screen showed a spreadsheet: the work the automations were replacing already happened in one.
nodes.source_quote: we jumped through like random locations and 99% of the time when you like open their loom it's like in a spreadsheet

nodes.label: 2M impressions, thousands of users
nodes.text: A week after release: two million impressions and thousands of users joined immediately.
nodes.source_quote: There are 2 million impressions, thousands of users joined immediately.

nodes.label: Demand from firms w/o finance team
nodes.text: The people using it include founders, VCs and small-business owners who do not have a large finance team: a population Ramp's internal pilot never contained.
nodes.source_quote: there is a real demand here, especially with founders, VCs, small businesses, especially owners of small businesses, they don't actually have a large finance team, right?

nodes.label: Wanted to see how people used it
nodes.text: Before the public release the team's stated expectation was that they had built a cool tool and wanted to see how people would play with it. No outcome is predicted.
nodes.source_quote: we thought we built a pretty cool tool and just wanted to see how people would play around with it.

nodes.label: Pivot to a spreadsheet interface
nodes.text: The team decided to meet the finance team where it already worked and build a spreadsheet interface instead of an automation layer.
nodes.source_quote: so we decided we should like really meet them where they work and have a spreadsheet interface for this.

nodes.label: Shipped shareable links
nodes.text: On the day of the interview the team shipped shareable links, with templates and an integration with Ramp's own spending data named as what comes next.
nodes.source_quote: We actually shipped shareable links today.

nodes.label: Derived: automate and they adopt
nodes.text: The unstated prediction the first pilot was testing: that if the finance team's own workflows were mined from video and rebuilt as Zapier and Retool automations, the team would adopt them and stop doing the work by hand.
nodes.rationale: The speaker says an experiment was run and describes exactly what was built and that they tried to get the finance team to use it. A pilot aimed at adoption implies the prediction that adoption would follow; the prediction itself is never said, which is why it has to be reconstructed before the refusal can count as a result.

nodes.label: Derived: generalises beyond Ramp
nodes.text: The unstated prediction of the second turn: that a spreadsheet which needed no Google or Excel account would be used outside Ramp's own finance team, by people who are not Ramp customers.
nodes.rationale: The stated plan is only to see how people play with the tool, yet the release was deliberately open to non-customers and the measurements reported afterwards are all reach. The prediction being tested is legible from the design of the release and from what the team chose to count.

nodes.label: Derived metric: would they use it?
nodes.text: The measure the first pilot was actually read against: whether the finance team used the automations. No target and no number, so a refusal is the whole of the result.
nodes.rationale: The only outcome reported for the automations is that the users would not use them, and the speaker frames the pilot as trying to get them to use it. Adoption by the pilot population is therefore the implicit measure, reconstructed because none was declared.

nodes.label: Derived metric: reach, no target
nodes.text: The measure the public release was read against: volume of reach - impressions, users joined, sheets created. Nothing was compared with a prediction, so no number here could have come out wrong.
nodes.rationale: Three quantities are reported and no threshold, baseline or expectation accompanies any of them. Naming reach as the implicit metric is what exposes the gap: the Check phase of this turn cannot falsify anything, which is the honest finding about it.

nodes.label: Standardise: ship into the surface
nodes.text: The rule the pivot standardises for the next bet: ship into the surface the measurement says the work already happens on, rather than asking the users to move to a new one. Stated as one product decision, not yet as a standard.
nodes.rationale: The team measured where the work happened, found one answer at 99 per cent, and changed the product to sit there. Reading that as a repeatable rule rather than a one-off fix is the generalisation the Act phase exists to make, and the source stops one step short of making it.
nodes.idea: Finance and back-office AI sells better as a spreadsheet that writes the model than as an agent that replaces the spreadsheet: the wedge is the surface the work is already recorded on, which is checkable by sampling recordings of the work.

nodes.label: Act on the segment that showed up
nodes.text: The decision the measurements point to and the team has not taken: aim the product at the population the release found - founders, VCs and owners of small businesses with no finance team - rather than at the finance team it was built for.
nodes.rationale: The pilot population was Ramp's own finance team; the adopters named after release have no finance team at all, and the speaker calls that real demand. Treating the new population as the target is a decision the Act phase owes the measurement, and the source names only features as next steps.
nodes.idea: An underserved segment: founders, VCs and small-business owners with no finance team who need a pro-forma or budget model in minutes and today pay a consultant thousands for a one-off template - a templated, instantly generated model layer priced for people who will never hire an analyst.

edges.rationale: Process mining is the first half of the thing being tried; linking it to the reconstructed prediction is an inference, because the speaker names no prediction for it to test.

The automations plus the attempt to get the team to use them are exactly what the reconstructed hypothesis predicts the outcome of, so this is the edge that makes the pilot an experiment rather than a build.
No measure was declared for the automations; adoption is inferred as the measure from the fact that getting the team to use them was the stated aim.
The refusal is the value the inferred adoption measure returned. The edge is derived because the measure it reads from is itself an inference.

edges.source_quote: we tried to get them to use it and they were like no this is too black box we can't really use this we need visibility into it
edges.label: and they were like no

edges.source_quote: tried to look through the looms of like all the information that they were giving to us and we jumped through like random locations and 99% of the time
when you like open their loom it's like in a spreadsheet so we decided we should like really meet them where they work
edges.label: so we decided

edges.rationale: The refusal is what sent the team back to the recordings in the first place, so it drives the pivot as much as the 99 per cent does; the source states the second link and not this one.

The spreadsheet interface chosen at the end of the first turn is the thing the second turn puts in front of strangers, and the speaker says the product went through many iterations. The cycle turning here is a reading of the narrative order.
An open release to non-customers is the trial of the reconstructed prediction that the tool generalises beyond the original pilot population.
Reach is inferred as the measure from the three quantities the team chose to report; no measure was agreed before the release.
The impression and user counts are the values the inferred reach measure returns; the edge is derived because the measure is.

edges.source_quote: So we released it last week and then the response was overwhelming. There are 2 million impressions, thousands of users joined immediately.
edges.label: the response was

edges.rationale: Who the adopters turned out to be is part of what the reach measure returned, and it is the part that carries the market information.
Shipping shareable links the same week follows the reach result and fits it, but the speaker gives no reason for the feature, so the link is plausible rather than stated.
The 99 per cent is the only evidence the generalised rule rests on; treating one sampled population as a rule for the next bet is the step beyond what was measured.
The named demand from firms without a finance team is what a retargeting decision would be read off; the source reports the demand and stops.
